title: Matthew 13:31–35
context: Jesus adds twin kingdom images—mustard seed and leaven—then Matthew explains His parable method as fulfillment of prophetic speech that utters what has been hidden.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Historic words on the mustard seed, the leaven, and why Jesus speaks in parables—so each camp speaks in its own voice beside Matthew 13:31–35.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: He proposed to them another parable - The former parables relate chiefly to unfruitful hearers; these that follow, to those who bear good fruit. The kingdom of heaven - Both the Gospel dispensation, and the inward kingdom. The least - That is, one of the least: a way of speaking extremely common among the Jews.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament (on Matt 13:31–35)

reformed.quote: All these things Jesus spoke in parables. Though Mark expressly says, that Christ spoke the word to them as they were able to bear it, yet I think it probable that he continued to employ parables, not so much for the purpose of instruction, as to keep the attention of his hearers awake till a more convenient time.
reformed.source: Commentary on a Harmony of the Evangelists (on Matt 13:31–35)

verses.text: He put another parable before them, saying, “The kingdom of heaven is like a grain of mustard seed that a man took and sowed in his field.
verses.arminianNotes:
The kingdom is likened to a mustard seed a man took and sowed. Small beginnings are not failures; they are the kingdom’s chosen scale.

Arminian encouragement: do not despise tiny starts. Grace often works through what looks insignificant so that hearers may trust the Sower rather than spectacle.
verses.reformedNotes:
Christ chooses a seed image again: taken and sown in a field. The kingdom’s advance is under the man’s intentional act.

Reformed hope: God authors small starts that belong to His purpose. The field is not random; the sowing is appointed.

verses.text: It is the smallest of all seeds, but when it has grown it is larger than all the garden plants and becomes a tree, so that the birds of the air come and make nests in its branches.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Smallest seed, surprising growth, shelter for birds. The kingdom outgrows its first appearance and becomes refuge.

Classical Arminians hear an invitation to patient faith: receive the word now, even when results look slight. Grace grows what we cannot inflate by force.
verses.reformedNotes:
Disproportion is the point: least seed, great plant, nesting branches. God delights to magnify His kingdom beyond human scale.

Reformed confidence: growth is God’s doing. The tree’s size and hospitality display His purpose, not human branding.
verses.keyContrast: Both celebrate surprising kingdom growth from small beginnings. Arminians typically stress patient, grace-enabled trust in the word sown; Reformed readers typically stress God’s sovereign power to enlarge what He plants.

verses.text: He told them another parable. “The kingdom of heaven is like leaven that a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, till it was all leavened.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Leaven hidden in flour works until all is leavened. The kingdom’s influence can be quiet, pervasive, and thorough.

Arminian pastoral reading: grace transforms from within as the word is received. Hidden does not mean inactive; it means steadily changing the whole.
verses.reformedNotes:
A woman hides leaven in a large batch until everything is changed. The kingdom’s work is often unseen before it is total.

Reformed emphasis: God effects thorough change by His appointed means. The “till” points to a sure outcome under His hand.

verses.text: All these things Jesus said to the crowds in parables; indeed, he said nothing to them without a parable.
verses.arminianNotes:
Matthew summarizes: Jesus spoke these things to the crowds in parables—indeed, nothing without a parable. The method is consistent, not occasional.

Arminian note: revelation is still being offered publicly. Parables keep inviting hearers to lean in, ask, and receive understanding by grace.
verses.reformedNotes:
The evangelist stresses Jesus’ settled parabolic address to the crowds. Form matches mission.

Reformed framing: Christ’s speech is purposeful under Scripture’s plan. He is not experimenting; He is fulfilling a pattern.

verses.text: This was to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet: “I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter what has been hidden since the foundation of the world.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Parables fulfill prophetic speech: opening the mouth to utter what was hidden. Jesus discloses mysteries in a form that both reveals and searches hearts.

Arminian wonder: what was hidden is now uttered. Grace brings light into history; hearers are called to receive what God has made known in the Son.
verses.reformedNotes:
Matthew cites fulfillment: Jesus’ parables enact the prophet’s line about uttering hidden things from the foundation.

Reformed doxology: revelation is historically timed by God. What was hidden is spoken now because the Son has come according to plan.
verses.keyContrast: Both treat parable-speech as fulfilled revelation, not mere storytelling. Arminians typically emphasize the uttered word as sincere light inviting reception; Reformed readers typically emphasize God’s sovereign disclosure on His timetable through the Messiah.
